title: Scheduler backpressure and pod admit leak - playbook draft
content:
Summary:
This is a working playbook for an emergent class of incidents we've seen over the past 6 weeks where the kube-scheduler stops admitting a fraction of pods and the cluster exhibits prolonged scheduling latency. Symptoms look like a slow leak: pods pile up in Pending with "node(s) had no available memory"/"fit failure" messages even though nodes report <90% memory usage overall. We suspect a combination of scheduler backpressure + stale predicate cache + transient CNI allocation stalls causing delayed pod binding and CV throttles on worker nodes.

Why this doc exists (context):
- Multiple customer-facing services experienced degraded autoscaling behavior and request latencies ~2–4x p95 when this happened.
- Incidents are intermittent and hard to reproduce in dev.
- We need a concise on-call mitigation path and medium-term fixes (cache invalidation, scheduler tunables, CNI allocation timeouts).

Key observable signals (Grafana panels to check):
- kube_scheduler_schedule_attempts_total (per-scheduler) and schedule_attempts_duration_seconds: p95/p99 spikes
- pending_pods_by_reason (broken down by reason strings: InsufficientMemory, FitFailure, NodeAffinity)
- node_memory_working_set_bytes and node_memory_available_bytes (per-node)
- cni_ip_alloc_failures_total and cni_allocate_latency_seconds
- apiserver_etcd_request_latency_seconds and etcd_server_proposals_committed_total (for correlated api-server slowness)
- pod_start_time_seconds histogram for recently scheduled pods
- kubelet_eviction_events_total (evictions by node)

Detection / Alerting heuristics (quick):
1) Alert if cluster pending pods > 50 for > 5m and >30% of pending pods have reason=FitFailure or InsufficientMemory.
2) Alert if scheduler schedule_attempts p95 > 500ms for >2m and schedule_attempts failures increment by >10%.
3) Alert if CNI allocate_latency p95 > 200ms or allocate_failures > 1/min per AZ.

Immediate mitigation (on-call checklist - fast path):
1) Run: kubectl get pods -A -o wide | grep Pending and capture top 10 pending pods with reasons. Paste to incident channel.
2) If majority are FitFailure/InsufficientMemory: kubectl describe node <node> for nodes referenced and check kubelet logs for OOMKiller/eviction activity.
3) If nodes show healthy memory but pods still fail to fit: check CNI IP allocations: kubectl logs daemonset/cni-plugin -n kube-system --tail=200 and gcloud/az cli for VPC IP pool exhaustion in that subnet.
4) Temporary relief options (choose one in order):
   a) Scale up node pool by +1-2 nodes in the affected AZ (fastest). Command example: gcloud container node-pools resize <pool> --num-nodes <n+2> --zone <z>.
   b) If scaling is slow: cordon a node with high pod churn and drain low-priority pods (kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --pod-selector="priority<1000000" <node>) to redistribute pressure.
   c) If CNI allocation is the bottleneck, restart the cni daemonset on one node to force re-sync: kubectl rollout restart daemonset/cni-plugin -n kube-system (do one AZ at a time).
5) If scheduler attempt latency is high across control-plane nodes: restart kube-scheduler on one replica (kubeadm/ops path) following safe restart procedure: cordon control-plane? (note: we have HA schedulers, restart sequentially).

Investigation timeline (example incident 2025-02-09):
- 09:42 UTC: Pager triggers - p95 scheduling latency > 800ms and 120 pending pods.
- 09:44 UTC: Oncall collects pending pod reasons: 70% InsufficientMemory, 20% FitFailure. Nodes appear to have 65–75% reported memory usage.
- 09:47 UTC: cni allocate_latency p95 spike to 450ms in us-west1-a. cni logs show transient warp (ipam request timeout -> queued).
- 09:50 UTC: Scaled nodepool +2 in us-west1-a, one new node registered by 09:54, scheduler backlog cleared by 09:58.
- 10:10 UTC: Post-incident, some pods still cycled due to liveness, rollouts delayed.

Root cause hypotheses (ranked):
1) IPAM/CNI allocation cross-talk: when many pods simultaneously startup (autoscaler event), IPAM requests pile up and the CNI plugin queues requests; scheduler still attempts binding but kubelet rejects until IP present, producing fit failure-like symptoms.
2) Scheduler predicate cache staleness + long schedule_attempts latency: scheduler keeps believing some nodes can't fit pods until cache TTL expires. This is amplified if apiserver latency is intermittent.
3) Node-level kernel throttling (net/core/somethings) causing kubelet heartbeat jitter and transient resource accounting spikes which confuse the scheduler.

Evidence needed to confirm:
- Correlate timestamps between cni allocate requests and scheduler failures (trace IDs if available).
- Check scheduler metrics for cache hit/miss counters and policy expiration.
- Compare kubelet NodeStatus update timestamps (are updates delayed?)

Mitigation tasks (medium term):
- Implement CNI allocation circuit-breaker: if allocate_latency p95 > 200ms, make the autoscaler pause new nodegroup scale-ups for 30s and use conservative burst window. (owner: infra-networking)
- Add a metrics-derived scheduler cache invalidation signal: on large scale-up events force a targeted scheduler cache refresh or decrease TTL. (owner: eng-scheduler)
- Harden CNI IP pool monitoring and add prewarm capacity for high-QPS autoscale events (owner: infra-networking)
- Add a runbook step to safely restart cni-plugin per-AZ in a rolling pattern for recovery. Document the exact command and timeout. (owner: eng-sre)

Permanent fixes and experiments (notes):
- Experiment A: tune kube-scheduler busy-loop backoff and score filter thresholds to reduce repeated predicate evaluation cost under load. Use feature gates carefully in canary clusters first.
- Experiment B: add short-lived delayed-binding admission controller to smooth bursts (batch binding) — requires API surface changes and strong testing.
- Experiment C: quantify and lower the IPAM request fanout per node by batching container creates in the runtime (CRI shim) when possible.

Runbook appendix (commands and snippets):
- List top pending pods by reason: kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Pending -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.namespace}/{.metadata.name} {.status.conditions[*].message}\n' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 30
- Check scheduler latency: kubectl -n kube-system port-forward svc/kube-scheduler-metrics 10254:10254 && curl localhost:10254/metrics | grep schedule_attempts_duration_seconds
- Restart cni daemonset one node at a time: for node in $(kubectl get nodes -l topology.kubernetes.io/zone=us-west1-a -o name); do kubectl cordon $node; kubectl delete pod -n kube-system -l name=cni-plugin --field-selector spec.nodeName=${node}; sleep 30; kubectl uncordon $node; sleep 60; done
- Safe kube-scheduler restart (HA): ssh to control-plane node, systemctl restart kube-scheduler (or kubectl delete pod -n kube-system <scheduler-pod> if running as pod) and monitor schedule_attempts metrics for recovery.

Post-incident action items (owners & ETA):
- infra-networking: add ipam saturation alert + runbook entry (ETA 2w) — Diego Morales
- eng-scheduler: prototype cache-invalidator on scale events (ETA 3w) — Rina Kapoor
- eng-sre: publish condensed on-call checklist and slack autosuggest message template (ETA 1w) — Aisha Patel

Open questions / TODOs:
- Do we have traces linking api-server request latency to CNI IPAM RPC calls? (observability)
- Should the autoscaler be aware of CNI saturation signals and reduce launch rate? (policies)
- Document safe thresholds for node cordon/drain when backpressure exists (avoid amplifying churn).

Notes to self / scribbles:
- Be careful with words "fit failure" vs "ipam delay" in alerts—mixing them loses signal.
- Consider quick patch to add pending_reason label enrichment in kube-state-metrics for easier grouping.

Related tickets / followups:
- JIRA-SRE-8421: Incident review and customer impact summary (link above)
- GH-617: initial ipam retry improvements PR

If you're reading this during an incident: focus on the detection heuristics above and pick the least invasive mitigation first. Update the incident channel with the top 3 signals and assigned owner immediately.

-- end of playbook draft (WIP)
